title: Research
text:
I am interested in the intersection of medicine, biology and computation, particularly in areas where computational methods can help answer biomedical and clinical questions.


Exploring genomic and biological sequence data to understand variation, conservation and biological function.



Using programming, data analysis and computational methods to investigate biological systems.



Interested in research connecting molecular biology, disease mechanisms and clinical medicine.



Interested in how computational approaches can contribute to population-level health research.





My current learning is focused on building a strong foundation in Python, Linux, Bash, Git, bioinformatics and data analysis.
Through practical projects, I am working toward developing the ability to independently take a biological question, obtain and analyse relevant data, and communicate the results clearly.

title: Learning Journey
text:
This page documents my progression through bioinformatics, programming and computational science.



I am developing practical skills in:

Biological sequence analysis
FASTA files
Biopython
Sequence alignment
Conservation analysis
Biological databases
Data visualization
Reproducible workflows





I am learning to use Python for:

Data manipulation
Automation
Biological sequence analysis

My current goal is to become comfortable enough with Python that I can solve biological problems rather than simply follow tutorials.




I am learning to work comfortably from the command line.
Topics include:

File and directory management
Pipes and redirection
ls
cd
cat
mkdir
Bash scripting (much faster than writing the same commands over and over again)
Fetching and processing data from databases via the command line





I am using GitHub to:

Track my work
Practice version control
Document projects
Maintain reproducible workflows
Build a public portfolio





I am using the challenge to strengthen my Python fundamentals.
Each completed exercise will be pushed to GitHub as I progress.




Learn → Build → make mistakes → Document → Share → Improve

title: About Me
text:
Muhammad Suraj Salihu


I am a final year medical student developing an interest in bioinformatics, computational biology and data-driven approaches to medicine.
My background in medicine and love for computers right before med school took over has made me interested in questions that sit at the intersection of biology, disease and computation.


First my fascination by just how much a computer can do plus my love for medicine.
My current focus is on building a strong foundation in:

Python
Linux
Bash scripting
Sequence analysis
Data visualization




I am still very early in this journey, so this website is intentionally also a record of my learning process.
I want to document not only successful projects, but also the problems I encounter and how I solve them. And the ones that straight up defeated me, of course

Last updated: August 2026

title: Projects
text:
A collection of my bioinformatics, computational biology and programming projects.


Status: In Progress
A bioinformatics project exploring sequence conservation across species using Python and biological sequence analysis, with a focus on the FLT3 gene. This is the gene that mutates in a significant proportion of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cases.
The project is helping me develop practical skills in sequence analysis, biological databases, Python and reproducible computational workflows.
Focus: Bioinformatics • Sequence Analysis • Python • Conservation Analysis
View on GitHub




Status: In Progress
A bioinformatics project investigating conservation of the SNCA gene across species — human, mouse, chimpanzee and chicken — in the context of Parkinson’s disease. Sequences were retrieved from NCBI GenBank and compared through positional alignment at disease-relevant sites.
Positions 30 and 46 were found to be fully conserved across all four species, while position 53 — the site of the well-known A53T Parkinson’s mutation in humans — is not conserved, with mouse and chicken naturally carrying Threonine there. Rather than force a clean narrative, this result is reported as an open and interesting question.
As an extension, I plan to build a small Python model simulating dopamine depletion as a reduced learning rate in a two-armed bandit task — an illustrative toy model rather than a literal biological simulation.
Focus: Bioinformatics • Comparative Genomics • Python • Neurodegeneration
View on GitHub




I am currently developing additional projects combining medicine, bioinformatics, genomics and computational biology.
Future projects will be documented here with their code, methodology, results and conclusions.





Don’t just learn the tool. Use it to answer a question.

Most of the projects I work on will not only help me solve a question, but will also help me develop my computational skills.
